scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Nos lowen developed in Cornwall during the 1990s, emerging roughly twenty years after the general revival of Cornish dancing had taken root.
It arose partly as a reaction to the more formal conventions of the earlier revival's social dance event, the troyl, which patterned itself after Scottish or Irish cèilidhs.
Looking across the English Channel for alternative cultural inspiration, organizers looked to the Breton fest noz, a participatory folk model that had surged in Brittany during the 1960s.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Meaning 'happy night' in the Cornish language, nos lowen serves as a celebratory social event designed to foster community cohesion and celebrate Cornish-Celtic identity.
The gathering format offers an inclusive alternative to caller-dependent dances, inviting spontaneous collective movement.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The initial nos lowen movement was spearheaded by the Cornish musical ensemble Sowena working with traditional dancers.
Other prominent musical proponents who have shaped the movement's sound include Dalla, Tredanek, Davey & Dyer, and Heb Mar.
The style is native to Cornwall.

Nos lowen is rooted in older Cornish dance traditions, specifically drawing on ancient forms such as the furry dance and snake dances, while adopting the event structure of the Breton fest noz of the 1960s.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Nos Lowen is influence of Fest noz: Nos lowen was directly inspired by the Breton fest noz format that emerged in the 1960s.
Nos Lowen is sibling of Troyl: Nos lowen developed partly as a reaction to the troyl, offering a caller-free alternative while both celebrate Cornish dance.
Nos Lowen is variant of Cèilidh: The earlier troyl was styled after Scottish and Irish ceilidhs, which nos lowen diverged from by eliminating the caller.
Nos Lowen is same region of Noson llawen: A related Welsh Celtic cultural gathering format sharing similar Celtic linguistic roots.
